rv.q: Given a wickedly sly look by scenic designer Miriam Buether (all that Trump Tower gold can’t be unintentional), this Lear is a knock-out.
Glenda Jackson was great fun, but, really, Lear shouldn't be great fun.
Shakespeare's mighty masterpiece has a way of forging an emotionally wrenching path into the heart and mind even through the thickest of directorial inventions, and that is largely the case here.
Jackson fails to wring tears, let alone blood, from this production, the sheer intelligence of her performance makes it memorable.

All these caveats notwithstanding, there can be no such thing as an ideal “Lear,” and the best parts of this admittedly uneven production are so distinguished that you should make haste to see it if you possibly can.

"A radical, enigmatic and uneven production that nonetheless showcases one of the great actresses of the stage, an octogenarian possessed of such energetic intensity and rhetorical accuracy as to seem almost superhuman.

It's often said that there's no greater grief than a parent's loss of a child, so it follows that there's no more devastating moment in King Lear than when the monarch's pitiless odyssey through familial betrayal, rage and madness, triggered by his own blind vanity, leaves him cradling the dead body of the one daughter whose love for him was pure.
But much of what surrounds her in this glittery, haphazard production seems to be working overtime to divert attention from that performance.
But if this revival represents a step forward for Gold’s career, it is a step backward for Shakespeare’s play, which has lost much of its excruciating pathos in the directorial hubbub.
Running three and a half hours (padding out the folio with bits of the quarto, like the mock trial scene), the production brings avant-garde techniques to Broadway with variable success.
But after three and a half hours of diffuse dramatics, I felt nothing.
Like so much else in this aggravating scrimmage of a “Lear,” the dimensions are off.
After a royal amount of hype built on the promise of the towering Glenda Jackson's role-defining performance, the painful truth is that Sam Gold's King Lear is a hot, heavy mess.
The new Broadway production of King Lear is a gripping presentation of a classic, with stellar performances by a formidable star and cast and assertive immediacy in its direction and design.
It is this returning veteran in the title role that makes this Lear memorable.

"A 'King Lear' that wholly captures the complexities and contradictions of its title character, a still-roaring lion who refuses to accept that winter has dawned. Gold’s production is at once a clever reflection of a culturally diverse modern world and a renunciation of the way ossified power structures are sustained...
For an actress who has always eschewed vanity, Lear has clearly provided a prize worth relishing—for her and for us.
To sum up, this is indeed a not to be missed star turn by Jackson, with enough positive assets to overcome the directorial missteps.
If Jackson’s performance turns this inventive but imperfect production into a must-see of the Broadway Spring season, it’s not just because of her impressive stamina and control.
Its only fault, and it was a significantly intrusive one for this critic, is a group of musicians who for some unknown, deeply grating reason, have been stationed at the back of the stage.

Ultimately, it's a thorny proposition if you want to spend the considerable time and money needed to see Jackson's crowning performance (and, possibly, her final Broadway appearance). But you'll likely feel like a fool if you don't.
Too bad that her frisky, wholly original performance seems to be going head-to-head with a director intent on imposing conceptual devices at every turn.

“Shakespeare’s patriarchal power play gets a Broadway reboot, thanks to Jackson’s star turn in the title role. But if you’re expecting a literal gender-bending commentary...Gold’s slick and somewhat stoic production might leave you with more questions than answers...
Conceptually, I see where Gold is going but as executed it comes off as amateurish.
Beginning with the famous storm sequence, her transition into Lear’s state of madness is underwhelming.
Without Lear at the center, the production fails to cohere into a well-defined whole and becomes a long three-and-a-half hour trek without a fulfilling payoff.
If you’re there to see Jackson, you won’t be disappointed.
But Gold’s listless production keeps dragging just when it should be gaining momentum.
Gold's rendition is a mixed bag with as many moving moments as confusing ones.
Glenda Jackson in Sam Gold’s King Lear is never dull but like the uneven production is never memorable except for the wrong reasons.

But when it doesn’t, which is, unfortunately, most of the time, it not only reveals the shortcomings of the Trump reference to begin with, but also the limitations of any approach to Shakespeare saddled to such an unsubtle allegory.
What also ensues is the madness that takes place on stage.
It’s a muddle of a production because Sam Gold, the director, seems to have thrown every idea he’s ever had at it and then left the room.
Staged at a stately pace, with an uneven company, grating music, and a star in her own personal universe, this is not a 'Lear' for the ages.
I heartily recommend a visit to this unique world before it closes July 7.
She’s a force of nature, and a King among Kings in the history of this iconic play.
Some of the cast members are good, but the production lacks distinction.
Go for Ms. Jackson, bewilder at the rest.

"The dominant color in Lear's court is gold; a porcelain bulldog and lion straddle the throne. These choices, with their whiff of Art Deco, are no doubt topical, though never fully explored: the text, about the dissolution of ancient Britain, doesn't really speak to our current political moment, and that's okay.
But the befuddling King Lear that opened at the Cort Theatre tonight is, to put it bluntly (and perhaps generously), a hot mess.
Overall, this production is a sorry mess and cannot be recommended.
At the end, as the deaths and gimmicks pile up around King Lear, it’s impossible not to view the proceedings as a showcase for anything but the play.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: Jackson's ferocious performance at 82 electrifies this production, but critics find Sam Gold's direction cluttered and uneven. Reviews praise the star's commanding presence while faulting the staging's gimmicks and lack of cohesion.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
